title: Orsen and the Winter
premise: Cyrus Montrose, an urban explorer who documents forgotten spaces, discovers a network of tunnels beneath her late grandmother's house that appear on no survey—and realizes the photographs from her childhood now contain an extra chair that was never there. The chair belongs to something her grandmother once invited in to keep the family safe, a bargain renewed each winter solstice, and this year no one renewed it. As the house seals itself against dawn and the tunnels fill with the thing's kin, Cyrus must choose between exposing the truth about her grandmother's vigilante justice—her grandmother lured predators into the tunnels as offerings—or completing the ritual herself. She holds out until sunrise by confessing the truth aloud, breaking the bargain but inheriting the duty: the door is counted, the lights are on, and now it's her turn.
about_author: S. M. Voss is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade mapping basements and service tunnels in old industrial cities, collecting the stories maintenance crews only tell after midnight. Voss writes horror about obligations we inherit from people who loved us badly and well at once.

chapters.title: The Doors Are Counted
chapters.summary: Cyrus, POV first person, finishes mapping a decommissioned waterworks, establishing her rituals: lights on, doors counted, nothing left open. A text summons her home—grandmother Edith has died, and the house is hers. Emotional beat: grief braided with the comfort of routine, and a faint wrongness she can't name yet.

chapters.title: What the Survey Doesn't Show
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Sorting Edith's papers, she finds hand-drawn tunnel maps beneath the house that match no city record, annotated with dates and names. Her friend Dev, a fellow explorer, confirms the tunnels aren't on any survey. Beat: curiosity curdling—the maps list names of missing people.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Cyrus compares childhood photographs of grandma's kitchen; every one, across forty years, includes a plain wooden chair no one remembers owning. In the newest photo—taken last week—the chair sits closer to the camera. Beat: quiet dread, the sense of being watched through the past.

chapters.title: Dev Descends
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Against Cyrus's rules, he enters the tunnel mouth behind the root cellar with a headlamp and a running GPS log. He finds the passage longer than the lot allows, walls hung with small bells. His log later shows eleven minutes he cannot account for. Beat: bravado curdling into violation.

chapters.title: Eleven Minutes
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Dev returns changed—polite, flat-eyed, insisting he was gone twenty minutes when his watch says thirty-one. He keeps glancing at the kitchen doorway where the wooden chair now physically sits. Beat: loyalty strained; Cyrus must decide whether to believe him or fear him.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: Cyrus finds a ledger hidden under floorboards: decades of entries pairing names with dates—men who hurt people and were never caught, each followed by 'taken below' and a tally mark. Justice outside the law, administered by her grandmother. Beat: horror and terrible pride tangled together.

chapters.title: The Terms of the Invitation
chapters.summary: A neighbor, Mrs. Okonkwo, who helped Edith, explains the bargain: something old lives below; Edith fed it the guilty, and it kept the town's worst impulses caged. The invitation must be renewed each solstice with spoken consent. This solstice is in three days. Beat: the weight of inheritance.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Furious at being handed a life sentence, Cyrus refuses to renew anything and plans to seal the tunnels permanently. The house responds: doors uncount themselves, lights fail room by room, and the chair moves nearer whenever she looks away. Beat: defiance meeting consequence.

chapters.title: Bells in the Dark
chapters.summary: Dev's POV, increasingly not-Dev. He walks the tunnels at night without remembering deciding to, ringing the wall-bells like a dinner bell. Below, something answers. Beat: dread of a friend becoming a door.

chapters.title: The Kin Come Up
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Things wearing the shapes of the ledger's names surface in the yard, polite and patient, asking to be let in because 'the table isn't set.' She counts doors; there are more than yesterday. Beat: siege begins; belonging weaponized—they claim she's one of them by blood.

chapters.title: Holding the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Cyrus barricades the kitchen, the oldest room, where the chair waits. She learns the rules empirically: salt on thresholds slows them, spoken truth strengthens the walls, lies make the lights gutter. Beat: resourcefulness under pressure; the theme crystallizes—truth as literal shelter.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Confession
chapters.summary: Through the boarded window, Mrs. Okonkwo admits she chose some of the names—people who hurt her daughter—and asks Cyrus's forgiveness before the things take her back inside. Beat: grief, complicity, and the cost of private justice; the moral center of the book.

chapters.title: What Dev Saw Down There
chapters.summary: A flicker of the real Dev surfaces long enough to describe what's below: a long table, many chairs, and Edith's own chair among them—she never left; she stayed as part of the price. Beat: heartbreak; the bargain cost Edith everything, willingly.

chapters.title: The Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Shortest day. Power fails for good. The things stop asking politely and begin testing every door in sequence, patient as tide. She counts forty-one doors; the house has nine. Beat: terror of arithmetic failing; time compressing toward sunrise.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The eldest of them speaks through the dead radio: sit in the chair, say yes, and everyone lives—including Dev, restored. It shows her Edith, seated below, waiting sixty years for company. Beat: temptation rendered intimate; loneliness as leverage.

chapters.title: Loyalty vs. Truth
chapters.summary: Cyrus nearly says yes—for Dev, for Edith, for belonging. Instead she speaks the whole truth aloud: what Edith did, what Mrs. Okonkwo did, what she herself wanted. Every lie she's told herself named. The walls blaze with light. Beat: climax pivot—truth as the only currency the thing respects.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: The things rage as dawn nears; the house itself fights for her, doors slamming in sequence like a heartbeat. Dev, half-free, drags himself to the threshold and chooses to stay below in her place unless she claims him by name and truth. Beat: sacrifice offered and refused.

chapters.title: Claimed by Name
chapters.summary: Cyrus speaks Dev's full name and the true story of their friendship into the collapsing dark; the claiming pulls him back over the threshold as the first light hits the windows. The things recede down the stairwell, unhurried, certain. Beat: release, exhaustion, love proven.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Morning. The kitchen chair remains, but now it faces the cellar door like a sentry post. The ledger's last page is blank except for fresh ink: her name, undated. Beat: hollow victory; the duty didn't die, it transferred.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dark
chapters.summary: Cyrus and Dev, recovering, debate burning the house or keeping the covenant. They visit the families the ledger's justice failed and succeeded for. Beat: moral reckoning; justice outside the law examined in daylight, unresolved but honest.

chapters.title: Renewal
chapters.summary: On the next solstice eve, Cyrus descends alone to the long table, sets Edith's chair upright, and speaks her renewal—not of the feeding, but of a new terms she dictates: the thing below will take only what is freely confessed, never the innocent, never the coerced. Something ancient considers, then assents. Beat: agency reclaimed; the myth rewritten.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Cyrus's POV, one year later. The photographs are normal again—except new ones show two chairs now, hers and a spare kept ready. She keeps the lights on, counts the doors, and waits for whoever inherits next. Last line lands on belonging chosen, not imposed. Beat: quiet, earned resolution with a held breath.
